Versality of algebraic group actions and rational points on twisted varietiesThanks: A. Duncan was partially supported by National Science Foundation RTG grants DMS 0838697 and DMS 0943832.Thanks: Z. Reichstein was partially supported by National Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada Discovery grant 250217-2012.

Alexander Duncan Address: Alexander Duncan
Department of Mathematics, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI 48109, USA and Zinovy Reichstein Address: Zinovy Reichstein
Department of Mathematics, University of British Columbia, Vancouver, BC V6T 1Z2, Canada
Abstract.

We formalize and study several competing notions of versality for an action of a linear algebraic group on an algebraic variety XX. Our main result is that these notions of versality are equivalent to various statements concerning rational points on twisted forms of XX (existence of rational points, existence of a dense set of rational points, etc.) We give applications of this equivalence in both directions, to study versality of group actions and rational points on algebraic varieties. We obtain similar results on pp-versality for a prime integer pp. An appendix, containing a letter from J.-P. Serre, puts the notion of versality in a historical perspective.

Key words and phrases: 
algebraic group, group action, torsor, versality, twisting, rational point, homogeneous space, universal torsor, toric variety, quadric, cubic hypersurface
2000 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 14L30, 14G05, Secondary 14M17, 14H10, 14M25

1. Introduction

Let kk be a base field and GG be a linear algebraic group defined over kk. We say that a GG-action on an irreducible kk-variety XX is

  • •

    weakly versal, if for every field K/kK/k, with KK infinite, and every GG-torsor T→Spec⁡(K)T\to\operatorname{Spec}(K) there is a GG-equivariant kk-morphism f:T→Xf\colon T\to X,

  • •

    versal, if every GG-invariant dense open subvariety of XX is weakly versal.

Note that here we view TT as a kk-scheme; it will not be of finite type in general. The advantage of the second notion over the first is that it only depends on XX up to (a GG-equivariant) birational isomorphism. In the case where X→BX\to B is a GG-torsor over some irreducible base space BB, our definition of versality is identical to [Ser03, Definition 5.1]. Versal and closely related “generic” objects (cf. Remark 2.8) naturally arise in many parts of algebra and algebraic geometry, such as the theory of central simple algebras [Pro67, Ami72, Sal99], Galois theory [JLY02], and the study of algebraic surfaces [Dun09, Tok06]. For a historical perspective we refer the reader to the appendix.

Our main result, Theorem 1.1 below, relates versality of XX to the existence of KK-points on certain KK-forms of XX, for field extensions K/kK/k. To state it, we need the following additional definitions, which will be used throughout the paper. We will say that a GG-action on XX is

  • •

    very versal, if there exists a linear representation G→GL⁡(V)G\to\operatorname{GL}(V) and a GG-equivariant dominant rational map V⇢XV\dasharrow X,

  • •

    birationally linear, if there exists a linear representation G→GL⁡(V)G\to\operatorname{GL}(V) and a GG-equivariant birational isomorphism between VV and XX,

  • •

    stably birationally linear, if there exists a linear representation G→GL⁡(W)G\to\operatorname{GL}(W) such that X×WX\times W is birationally linear.

If K/kK/k is a field extension, with KK infinite, and π:T→Spec⁡(K)\pi\colon T\to\operatorname{Spec}(K) is a GG-torsor, we will refer to (T,K)(T,K) as a twisting pair (see Definition 4.1) and write XT{}^{T}X for the KK-variety obtained by twisting XKX_{K} by TT (see Section 3).

Theorem 1.1.

Let GG be a linear algebraic group defined over kk. A GG-action on an irreducible quasiprojective kk-variety XX is

  1. (a)

    weakly versal if and only if, for every twisting pair (T,K)(T,K), XT​(K)≠∅\,{}^{T}X(K)\neq\emptyset,

  2. (b)

    versal if and only if, for every twisting pair (T,K)(T,K), KK-points are dense in XT\,{}^{T}X,

  3. (c)

    very versal if and only if, for every twisting pair (T,K)(T,K), XT\,{}^{T}X is KK-unirational,

  4. (d)

    stably birationally linear if and only if, for every twisting pair (T,K)(T,K), XT\,{}^{T}X is stably KK-rational.

Theorem 1.1 tells us, in particular, that for a GG-variety XX, the implications

(1.1) stably birationally linear ⟹\implies very versal ⟹\implies versal ⟹\implies weakly versal

cannot be reversed in general, even if G={1}G=\{1\}. Simple examples of versal GG-varieties XX that are not very versal can be constructed as follows. Suppose XX is versal. Then by the definition of versality X×kYX\times_{k}Y is also versal, for any variety YY with trivial GG-action, provided that kk-points are dense in YY. If YY is not unirational (e.g., is an elliptic curve), then X×kYX\times_{k}Y is not unirational and hence, cannot be very versal.

On the other hand, in many natural examples XX is geometrically unirational, i.e., XX becomes unirational over an algebraic closure k¯\bar{k}. In this situation the twisted KK-variety XT{}^{T}X is geometrically unirational for every twisting pair (T,K)(T,K). For a smooth geometrically unirational variety YY defined over an infinite field KK, it is not known whether or not the following properties are equivalent: (i) YY is KK-unirational, (ii) KK-points are dense in YY, and (iii) YY has a KK-point; see [Kol02, Question 1.3]. It is thus conceivable that if XX is smooth and geometrically unirational then the second and third implications in (1.1) may, indeed, be reversed. This explains why part (b) of Theorem 1.1, which takes the most delicate arguments to prove, is never truly used in the specific examples in this paper, i.e., why versal varieties in these examples turn out to be very versal.

The rest of this paper is structured as follows. Section 2 is devoted to notation and preliminaries, and Section 3 to a discussion of the twisting operation. In Sections 4 and 5 we prove Theorem 1.1. In Section 6 we show that every KK-form of the moduli spaces M¯0,n\overline{M}_{0,n} and M¯1,n\overline{M}_{1,n} are unirational over KK for certain nn. In Section 7 we use Theorem 1.1 in the other direction to give a versality criterion for the action of a closed subgroup G⊂AG\subset A on a homogeneous space A/BA/B. In Section 8 we define and study the related notions of pp-versality, where pp is a prime integer. We show that pp-versality is related to 00-cycles on twisted varieties (rather than points) and that for smooth varieties, weak pp-versality is equivalent to pp-versality. Sections 9 and 10 feature versality criteria for group actions on projective spaces and low degree hypersurfaces. As an application, we show that a recent conjecture of I. Dolgachev on the Cremona dimension is incompatible with a long-standing conjecture of J. W. S. Cassels and P. Swinnerton-Dyer about rational points on cubic hypersurfaces.

2. Notation and preliminaries

Let kk be a field; we will denote an algebraic closure of kk by k¯\bar{k}.

A kk-variety XX is a reduced, quasiprojective scheme of finite type over kk, not necessarily irreducible. A morphism of kk-varieties is a morphism of schemes respecting the structure morphism to kk. A product of kk-varieties is a fibre product of schemes over kk.

An algebraic group GG over kk is a smooth affine group scheme of finite type over kk. An action of GG on XX will always be a morphic action, i.e., a morphism σ:G×X→X\sigma:G\times X\to X satisfying the standard conditions [MFK94]. We will sometimes refer to XX with an action of GG as a GG-variety.

Given a kk-variety XX and a field extension K/kK/k, the symbol XKX_{K} denotes the KK-variety X×Spec⁡(k)Spec⁡(K)X\times_{\operatorname{Spec}(k)}\operatorname{Spec}(K). A kk-form of XX is a kk-variety X′X^{\prime} such that Xk¯≃Xk¯′X_{\bar{k}}\simeq X^{\prime}_{\bar{k}}.

A right (resp. left) GG-torsor over YY is a flat morphism ψ:X→Y\psi:X\to Y of kk-schemes such that GG acts on XX on the right (resp. left), and the map σ×π2:GY×YX→X×YX\sigma\times\pi_{2}:G_{Y}\times_{Y}X\to X\times_{Y}X is an isomorphism (where σ\sigma is the action map and π2\pi_{2} is the second projection). The set of GG-torsors over a field KK is in bijection with the Galois cohomology set H1​(K,G)H^{1}(K,G).

A kk-variety is rational if it is kk-birationally equivalent to 𝔸n{\mathbb{A}}^{n}, for some positive integer nn. A kk-variety XX is unirational if there exists a dominant rational kk-map 𝔸n⇢X{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\dasharrow X.

A GG-action on XX is generically free if there exists a dense GG-invariant open subvariety X0⊂XX_{0}\subset X such that the scheme-theoretic stabilizer of every point x∈X0x\in X_{0} is trivial. This is equivalent to the existence of a dense GG-invariant open subvariety UU of XX which is the total space of a GG-torsor π:U→B\pi:U\to B; see [BF03, Theorem 4.7]. If BB is irreducible, we say that XX is a primitive GG-variety.

Given a generically free primitive GG-variety XX one obtains a GG-torsor over Spec⁡(k⁡(B))\operatorname{Spec}(k(B)) by taking the generic fibre of π\pi. Conversely, given a GG-torsor over a finitely generated field extension K/kK/k, one can recover a birational equivalence class of generically free primitive GG-varieties for which k⁡(B)=Kk(B)=K. Indeed, the GG-torsor is an affine KK-variety and thus can be defined over some finitely generated kk-subalgebra of KK.

The following remark is an immediate consequence of this correspondence.

Remark 2.1.

A GG-action on an irreducible kk-variety XX is weakly versal if and only if, for every generically free primitive GG-variety YY defined over kk, with k​(Y)Gk(Y)^{G} infinite, there exists a GG-equivariant kk-rational map Y⇢XY\dasharrow X.

Proposition 2.2.

Let XX be an irreducible GG-variety defined over kk. If GG has a fixed kk-point x∈X⁡(k)x\in X(k) then XX is weakly versal.

Proof.

For every field K/kK/k and every GG-torsor T→Spec⁡(K)T\to\operatorname{Spec}(K), the constant map T→XT\to X, sending all of TT to xx, is GG-equivariant. ∎

We will view a linear representation G→GL⁡(V)G\to\operatorname{GL}(V) of GG on a kk-vector space VV as a GG-action on the affine space associated to VV. By abuse of notation, we will denote this affine space by the same symbol VV. We will say that a linear representation G→GL⁡(V)G\to\operatorname{GL}(V) is generically free if the GG-variety VV is generically free. The GG-torsors U→BU\to B, associated to generically free linear representations G→GL⁡(V)G\to\operatorname{GL}(V), as above, will play an important role in this paper. Note that torsors of this form may be viewed as “algebraic approximations” to the universal torsor over the classifying space of GG, in the sense of B. Totaro [Tot99].

Remark 2.3.

Let GG be an algebraic group over kk. Then there exists a generically free linear representation G→GL⁡(V)G\to\operatorname{GL}(V); see [BF03, Remark 4.12]. Moreover, adding a copy of the trivial representation if necessary, we can choose VV so that k​(V)Gk(V)^{G} is an infinite field.

Remark 2.4.

It is vital that algebraic groups are linear throughout this paper. For example, if A≠{1}A\neq\{1\} is an abelian variety then no versal AA-torsor can exist. Otherwise the exponent of every element of H1​(K,A)H^{1}(K,A), for any field K/kK/k, would divide the exponent of the versal torsor. However, there are AA-torsors of arbitrarily high exponent (over suitable KK); cf. [Bro07, Section 3].

Proposition 2.5.

If XX is a versal irreducible GG-variety then XX is geometrically irreducible.

Proof.

It suffices to show that XksX_{k^{s}} is irreducible, where ksk^{s} denotes a separable closure of kk; see [Har77, Exercise 2.3.15(a)]. Let X1,…,XnX_{1},\dots,X_{n} denote the irreducible components of XksX_{k^{s}}. We want to show that n=1n=1. We will argue by contradiction. Assume n⩾2n\geqslant 2. Since XX is irreducible over kk, the absolute Galois group Gal⁡(k)\operatorname{Gal}(k) permutes X1,…,XnX_{1},\dots,X_{n} transitively. Thus Y:=X1∩⋯∩XnY:=X_{1}\cap\dots\cap X_{n} is a closed GG-invariant kk-subvariety of XX (possibly empty) and X≠YX\neq Y.

Let VV be a generically free linear GG-representation with k​(V)Gk(V)^{G} infinite. By Remark 2.1 there exists a GG-equivariant rational kk-map f:V⇢X∖Yf\colon V\dasharrow X\setminus Y. Since VV is geometrically irreducible, the image of ff is contained in one of the components XiX_{i}. Since Gal⁡(k)\operatorname{Gal}(k) transitively permutes the components, the image of ff is also contained in X2,…,XnX_{2},\dots,X_{n} and thus in YY, a contradiction. ∎

Remark 2.6.

Suppose XX is of minimal dimension among generically free versal GG-varieties. Then XX must be very versal. To see this, let VV be a generically free linear representation of GG, as in Remark 2.3. Let U⊂XU\subset X be a GG-invariant open subvariety which is the total space of a GG-torsor U→BU\to B. Then UU is weakly versal and, by Remark 2.1, there exists a GG-equivariant rational map f:V⇢Uf:V\dasharrow U. The closure ZZ of the image of ff is very versal and, since UU is a GG-torsor, the action on ZZ is generically free. By minimality of dim(X)\dim(X), we conclude that dim(Z)=dim(X)\dim(Z)=\dim(X) and thus ff is dominant.

The minimal value of dim(X)−dim(G)\dim(X)-\dim(G), as XX ranges over the very versal (or equivalently, versal) generically free GG-varieties, is called the essential dimension of GG and is denoted by ed⁡(G)\operatorname{ed}(G); see [BF03], [Ser03, Section 5] or [R10].

Remark 2.7.

The following criterion gives a convenient way (often the only known way) to show that a given action is not versal.

Let XX be a projective irreducible weakly versal GG-variety defined over kk. Suppose H⊂GH\subset G is a closed kk-subgroup such that every finite-dimensional kk-representation of HH has a 11-dimensional invariant subspace. Then XX has an HH-fixed kk-point.

In applications, HH is usually taken to be a finite constant abelian group. When kk has suitable roots of unity, every linear representation of such a group decomposes as a direct sum of 11-dimensional character spaces; in particular, the above criterion applies. For example, the usual action of the alternating group G=A5G=\operatorname{A}_{5} on X=ℙ1X={\mathbb{P}}^{1} (say, over the field k=ℂk={\mathbb{C}} of complex numbers) is not versal. Indeed, GG contains a subgroup HH isomorphic to ℤ/2​ℤ×ℤ/2​ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}/2{\mathbb{Z}}\times{\mathbb{Z}}/2{\mathbb{Z}} which has no fixed points in ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}. Here one generator of ℤ/2​ℤ×ℤ/2​ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}/2{\mathbb{Z}}\times{\mathbb{Z}}/2{\mathbb{Z}} takes (x:y)∈ℙ1(x:y)\in{\mathbb{P}}^{1} to (−x:y)(-x:y) and the other to (y:x)(y:x). Arguments of this type are used extensively, e.g., in [Dun09], [Dun10], [Bea11] and [Tok06].

To prove the criterion, let VV be a generically free GG-representation. By Remark 2.1, there is a GG-equivariant (and hence, HH-equivariant) rational map V⇢XV\dasharrow X. Since VV has a smooth HH-fixed point (the origin), the “Going Down Theorem” implies that XX has an HH-fixed point; see [RY00, Proposition A.2 and Remark A.7]. ∎

Remark 2.8.

The notion of a generic group action, in the sense of D. J. Saltman [Sal82], is closely related to our notion of versality but is not identical to it. The action of GG on an irreducible variety XX is called generic if it is generically free, versal and k​(X)Gk(X)^{G} is a rational (i.e., purely transcendental) field extension of kk. Note that while versal actions exist for every algebraic group GG, generic GG-actions may or may not exist, depending on GG. We also note that for a finite group GG the existence of a generic action is equivalent to the existence of a generic polynomial in the sense of F. DeMeyer [DM84, JLY02]. The distinction between “versal” and “generic” is often blurred in the literature.

3. Twisting

Let G/kG/k be an algebraic group, X/kX/k be a GG-variety, and T→Spec⁡(k)T\to\operatorname{Spec}(k) be a right GG-torsor. The diagonal action of GG on T×XT\times X makes T×XT\times X into the total space of a GG-torsor T×X→BT\times X\to B. The base space BB of this torsor is unique (it is the geometric quotient of T×XT\times X by GG); it is usually called the twist of XX by TT and denoted by XT{}^{T}X. This construction relies on our standing assumption that XX is quasiprojective; for details, see [Flo08, Section 2] or [CTKPR11, Section 2].

Note that there is no natural GG-action on XT{}^{T}X; we lose the GG-action in the course of constructing XT{}^{T}X. However, XT{}^{T}X carries a natural action of the twisted group GT{}^{T}G; see Propositions 3.5 and 3.6 below.

If TT is split over kk, it is easy to see that XT{}^{T}X is kk-isomorphic to XX. Hence, XT{}^{T}X is a kk-form of XX, i.e., XX and XT{}^{T}X become isomorphic over any splitting field L/kL/k of TT. Combining this observation with Hilbert’s Theorem 90 ([Ser79, Proposition X.1.3]), we obtain the following.

Lemma 3.1.

Let VV be a linear representation G→GL⁡(V)G\to\operatorname{GL}(V) and T→Spec⁡(k)T\to\operatorname{Spec}(k) be a GG-torsor. Then VT{}^{T}V is kk-isomorphic to VV. In particular, VT​(k){}^{T}V(k) is dense in VT{}^{T}V. ∎

It is well-known that quasiprojectivity is a geometric property, in the sense that if a kk-variety is quasiprojective over k¯\bar{k} then it is quasiprojective over kk. Thus, twisting is performed entirely within the category of quasiprojective varieties.

Twisting is functorial in the following sense: a GG-equivariant morphism f:X→Yf\colon X\to Y (respectively, a rational map f:X⇢Yf\colon X\dasharrow Y) of GG-varieties gives rise to a KK-morphism fT:XT→YT{}^{T}f\colon{}^{T}X\to{}^{T}Y (respectively, a KK-rational map fT:XT⇢YT{}^{T}f\colon{}^{T}X\dasharrow{}^{T}Y). For details, see [Flo08, Lemma 2.2] (where only rational maps are considered, but the construction of fT{}^{T}f is even more straightforward if ff is regular).

The following Proposition amplifies [CTKPR11, Lemma 3.4].

Proposition 3.2.

Let kk be a field, GG be an algebraic group and T→Spec⁡(k)T\to\operatorname{Spec}(k) be a GG-torsor. Denote by 𝐕𝐚𝐫\mathbf{Var} the category of kk-varieties and by G​-​𝐕𝐚𝐫G\textrm{-}\mathbf{Var} the category of kk-varieties with a GG-action. Morphisms in the latter category are GG-equivariant kk-maps.

Let ℒT:𝐕𝐚𝐫→G​-​𝐕𝐚𝐫\mathcal{L}_{T}:\mathbf{Var}\to G\textrm{-}\mathbf{Var} be the functor T×−T\times- which takes a kk-variety YY to T×YT\times Y (viewed as a GG-variety, with GG acting trivially on YY). Let ℛT:G​-​𝐕𝐚𝐫→𝐕𝐚𝐫\mathcal{R}_{T}:G\textrm{-}\mathbf{Var}\to\mathbf{Var} be the twisting functor (T−)(^{T}-) described above.

Then the functors (ℒT,ℛT)(\mathcal{L}_{T},\mathcal{R}_{T}) form an adjoint pair. In other words, for any Y∈𝐕𝐚𝐫Y\in\mathbf{Var} and X∈G​-​𝐕𝐚𝐫X\in G\text{-}\mathbf{Var}, we have an isomorphism

(3.1) HomG​-​𝐕𝐚𝐫⁡(T×Y,X)≃Hom𝐕𝐚𝐫⁡(Y,XT)\operatorname{Hom}_{G\textrm{-}\mathbf{Var}}(T\times Y,X)\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Var}}(Y,{}^{T}X)

which is functorial in both XX and YY.

Proof.

The isomorphism is easiest to see by considering the intermediate set ℱ⁡(Y,X)\mathcal{F}(Y,X) consisting of GG-equivariant morphisms γ:T×Y→T×X\gamma:T\times Y\to T\times X such that the following diagram commutes:

where the vertical maps are projections.

Given γ∈ℱ⁡(Y,X)\gamma\in\mathcal{F}(Y,X), we obtain α=pr2∘γ\alpha=\operatorname{pr}_{2}\circ\gamma in HomG​-​𝐕𝐚𝐫⁡(T×Y,X)\operatorname{Hom}_{G\textrm{-}\mathbf{Var}}(T\times Y,X). Mapping α∈HomG​-​𝐕𝐚𝐫⁡(T×Y,X)\alpha\in\operatorname{Hom}_{G\textrm{-}\mathbf{Var}}(T\times Y,X) to γ=pr1×α\gamma=\operatorname{pr}_{1}\times\alpha is an inverse. Given γ∈ℱ⁡(Y,X)\gamma\in\mathcal{F}(Y,X), we obtain β∈Hom𝐕𝐚𝐫⁡(Y,XT)\beta\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Var}}(Y,{}^{T}X) by taking quotients. All of these operations are clearly functorial.

It remains to reconstruct γ∈ℱ⁡(Y,X)\gamma\in\mathcal{F}(Y,X) given β:Y→XT\beta:Y\to{}^{T}X. Pulling back the GG-torsor T×X→XTT\times X\to{}^{T}X we obtain a GG-torsor π:Y′→Y\pi:Y^{\prime}\to Y:

The GG-equivariant map ϕ=(pr1∘f)×π\phi=(\operatorname{pr}_{1}\circ f)\times\pi is a morphism of GG-torsors ϕ:Y′→T×Y\phi:Y^{\prime}\to T\times Y over YY. By a standard result on torsors, this means ϕ\phi is an isomorphism.

Thus, we have a GG-equivariant morphism γ′=f∘ϕ−1:T×Y→T×X\gamma^{\prime}=f\circ\phi^{-1}:T\times Y\to T\times X which lifts β\beta. However, since pullbacks are only defined up to isomorphism, the projections T×Y→TT\times Y\to T and T×X→TT\times X\to T do not necessarily commute with γ′\gamma^{\prime}. Nevertheless, there exists a unique g∈Gg\in G such that g∘γ′g\circ\gamma^{\prime} is in ℱ⁡(Y,X)\mathcal{F}(Y,X). This is the desired γ\gamma. The construction is easily seen to be functorial. ∎

Corollary 3.3.

Let XX be a GG-variety, and T→Spec⁡(k)T\to\operatorname{Spec}(k) be a GG-torsor. Let L/kL/k be a splitting field of TT, let ss be a point in T⁡(L)T(L), and let ts:(XT)L→XLt_{s}:({}^{T}X)_{L}\to X_{L} be the LL-isomorphism such that s×tss\times t_{s} is a section of πL:TL×XL→(XT)L\pi_{L}:T_{L}\times X_{L}\to({}^{T}X)_{L}. If α:T→X\alpha\colon T\to X and β:Spec⁡(k)→XT\beta\colon\operatorname{Spec}(k)\to{}^{T}X are corresponding maps under the adjunction of Proposition 3.2 (with Y=Spec⁡(k)Y=\operatorname{Spec}(k)) then αL​(s)=ts​(βL)\alpha_{L}(s)=t_{s}(\beta_{L}) in X⁡(L)X(L).

Proof.

By definition, α\alpha and β\beta fit into the following commutative diagram of GG-equivariant kk-morphisms:

The vertical maps are GG-torsors; we split them by base-changing from kk to LL. By the definition of tst_{s} the resulting diagram

is commutative. Tracing from the lower left corner to the upper right, we see that s×αL​(s)=s×ts​(βL)s\times\alpha_{L}(s)=s\times t_{s}(\beta_{L}) as morphisms Spec⁡(L)→TL×XL\operatorname{Spec}(L)\to T_{L}\times X_{L}. Composing these morphisms with the projection TL×XL→XLT_{L}\times X_{L}\to X_{L}, we see that αL​(s)=ts​(βL)\alpha_{L}(s)=t_{s}(\beta_{L}) as maps Spec⁡(L)→X\operatorname{Spec}(L)\to X. ∎

Corollary 3.4.

Let XX and YY be GG-varieties defined over kk, and let T→Spec⁡(k)T\to\operatorname{Spec}(k) be a GG-torsor. Then

  1. (a)

    (X×Y)T{}^{T}(X\times Y) is canonically isomorphic to XT×YT{}^{T}X\times{}^{T}Y.

  2. (b)

    Let f:X→Yf\colon X\to Y be a GG-equivariant closed (resp. open) immersion. Then fT:XT→YT{}^{T}f\colon{}^{T}X\to{}^{T}Y is also a closed (resp. open) immersion.

  3. (c)

    If f:X⇢Yf\colon X\dasharrow Y is a GG-equivariant dominant rational map then the induced rational map fT:XT⇢YT{}^{T}f\colon{}^{T}X\dasharrow{}^{T}Y is also dominant.

Proof.

(a) follows from the fact that the twisting functor is a right adjoint and, thus, is left exact. To prove (b) and (c) note that by [EGA IV, Proposition 2.7.1] the properties of being a closed or open immersion and of being dominant are geometric. In other words, for the purpose of checking that fT{}^{T}f has these properties, we may pass to any field extension L/kL/k. In particular, we may replace kk by a splitting field of TT and thus assume without loss of generality that T→Spec⁡(k)T\to\operatorname{Spec}(k) is split. In this case XT{}^{T}X, YT{}^{T}Y and fT{}^{T}f become XX, YY, and ff, respectively, and the assertions of parts (b) and (c) become obvious. ∎

Proposition 3.5.

(cf. [CTKPR11, Lemma 3.5]) Suppose HH and GG are algebraic groups over kk, and GG acts on HH by group automorphisms. Let T→Spec⁡(k)T\to\operatorname{Spec}(k) be a GG-torsor. Then HT{}^{T}H is a kk-form of the algebraic group HH. In particular, HT{}^{T}H is an affine algebraic group over kk.

Proof.

The commutative diagrams defining the group scheme structure on HH are all GG-equivariant. Applying the twisting functor to these diagrams, and using Corollary 3.4(a), we see that HT{}^{T}H is an algebraic group. If L/kL/k is a splitting field of TT then clearly (TH)L(^{T}H)_{L} and HLH_{L} are isomorphic. The assertion that HH is affine follows by descent; see [EGA IV, Proposition 2.7.1(xiii)]. ∎

Proposition 3.6.

Let T→Spec⁡(k)T\to\operatorname{Spec}(k) be a GG-torsor and let GT{}^{T}G denote the twist by TT of the conjugation action of GG on itself. For every GG-variety XX, the GG-action on XX induces a GT{}^{T}G-action on XT{}^{T}X. Moreover, for every GG-equivariant morphism ff the morphism fT{}^{T}f is GT{}^{T}G equivariant. In other words, the twisting functor factors through the category of GT{}^{T}G-varieties.

Proof.

The action map G×X→XG\times X\to X and associated commutative diagrams are all GG-equivariant. As in the proof of Proposition 3.5, we obtain an action map GT×XT→XT{}^{T}G\times{}^{T}X\to{}^{T}X and commutative diagrams which show that fT{}^{T}f is GT{}^{T}G equivariant. ∎

4. Proof of Theorem 1.1(a) and (b)

We will use repeatedly the fact that twisting commutes with base field extension. Given a kk-variety XX, a field extension K/kK/k, and a GG-torsor T→Spec⁡(K)T\to\operatorname{Spec}(K), we will use the shorthand notation XT{}^{T}X to denote (XK)T{}^{T}(X_{K}).

For brevity, we use the following terminology throughout the paper.

Definition 4.1.

Let kk be a field and GG be an algebraic group over kk. By a GG-twisting pair (T,K)(T,K) we shall mean a choice of a field extension K/kK/k, with KK infinite, and a GG-torsor T→Spec⁡(K)T\to\operatorname{Spec}(K). In situations where the choice of GG is clear from the context and there is no risk of ambiguity, we will simply refer to (T,K)(T,K) as a twisting pair.

Proof of Theorem 1.1(a).

Let (T,K)(T,K) be any twisting pair. Setting Y=Spec⁡(K)Y=\operatorname{Spec}(K) in Proposition 3.2, we see that the KK-points of XT{}^{T}X are in a natural 1−11-1 correspondence with GG-equivariant maps T→XT\to X. ∎

The proof of Theorem 1.1(b) is considerably more delicate. Before we proceed with the details, we would like to explain a new obstacle our argument will have to overcome.

Given a GG-action on an irreducible XX, and a GG-twisting pair (T,K)(T,K), let us say that XX is (T,K)(T,K)-weakly versal if there exists a morphism T→XT\to X defined over kk. The GG-action on XX is, by definition, weakly versal if it is (T,K)(T,K)-weakly versal for every twisting pair (T,K)(T,K). Note that our proof of Theorem 1.1(a) establishes the following stronger statement:

Choose a GG-twisting pair (T,K)(T,K). Then an irreducible GG-variety XX is (T,K)(T,K)-weakly versal if and only if XT{}^{T}X has a KK-point.

Similarly, given a GG-twisting pair (T,K)(T,K), we will say that an irreducible GG-variety XX is (T,K)(T,K)-versal if every dense GG-invariant open subvariety of XX is (T,K)(T,K)-weakly versal. One is thus naturally led to try to prove Theorem 1.1(b) by showing that for any given GG-twisting pair (T,K)(T,K), XX is (T,K)(T,K)-versal if and only if KK-points are dense in XT{}^{T}X. The following example shows that this stronger version of Theorem 1.1(b) fails.

Example 4.2.

Let k=ℂk=\mathbb{C} and let XX be a smooth irreducible projective complex curve of genus g⩾2g\geqslant 2, whose automorphism group G:=Aut⁡(X)G:=\operatorname{Aut}(X) is non-trivial. By Hurwitz’s theorem, GG is finite.

Let π:X→X/G\pi\colon X\to X/G be the quotient map, let K:=k​(X)G=k⁡(X/G)K:=k(X)^{G}=k(X/G), and let T→Spec⁡(K)T\to\operatorname{Spec}(K) be the GG-torsor obtained by pulling back π\pi via the generic point Spec⁡(K)→X/G\operatorname{Spec}(K)\to X/G. Then the GG-action on XX is (T,K)(T,K)-versal, since the identity map X→XX\to X restricts to a GG-equivariant morphism T→UT\to U for any GG-invariant open subvariety U⊂XU\subset X.

On the other hand, we claim that the KK-curve XT{}^{T}X has only finitely many KK-points, and hence, KK-points cannot be dense in XT{}^{T}X. Indeed, arguing as in the proof of Theorem 1.1(a), we see that KK-points of XT{}^{T}X are in a natural bijective correspondence with GG-equivariant kk-morphisms T→XT\to X or equivalently, with GG-equivariant rational maps X⇢XX\dasharrow X, or equivalently (since XX is a smooth complete curve) with GG-equivariant morphisms X→XX\to X. The latter can be of two types: (i) dominant and (ii) constant (i.e., the image is a single point of XX). It thus suffices to show that there are only finitely many morphisms X→XX\to X of each type.

(i) Since g⩾2g\geqslant 2, the Hurwitz formula tells us that any dominant morphism X→XX\to X is, in fact, an automorphism of XX. As we mentioned above, XX has only finitely many automorphisms.

(ii) If the image of ff is a point of XX, this point has to be fixed by GG, and XX has only finitely many GG-fixed points. This completes the proof of the claim. ∎

The above example demonstrates that, given a twisting pair (T,K)(T,K), we cannot hope to deduce the density of KK-points in XT{}^{T}X merely from the fact that XX is (T,K)(T,K)-versal. When XX is versal, we will deduce the density of KK-points in XT{}^{T}X, for every twisting pair (T,K)(T,K), from the fact that, in particular, XX is (S,F)(S,F)-versal, where SS and FF are as follows.

Definition 4.3.

For the rest of this section and in Section 5:

  • •

    VV will denote a generically free linear representation of GG.

  • •

    FF will denote the field k​(V)Gk(V)^{G}. We will choose VV so that FF is infinite (see Remark 2.3).

  • •

    V0V_{0} will denote a dense open GG-invariant subvariety of VV which is the total space of a GG-torsor V0→BV_{0}\to B.

  • •

    S→Spec⁡(F)S\to\operatorname{Spec}(F) will denote the GG-torsor obtained by pulling back V0→BV_{0}\to B via the generic point η:Spec⁡(F)→B\eta\colon\operatorname{Spec}(F)\to B.

We now proceed with the proof of Theorem 1.1(b).

Lemma 4.4.

Let X/kX/k be a geometrically irreducible GG-variety, and suppose XX is (T,K)(T,K)-versal for some twisting pair (T,K)(T,K). Then, for any field extension L/kL/k and for any closed LL-subvariety Y⊊XLY\subsetneq X_{L} (not necessarily GG-invariant), there exists a GG-equivariant kk-morphism ψ:T→X\psi:T\to X such that the image of ψL:T×kSpec⁡(L)→XL\psi_{L}:T\times_{k}\operatorname{Spec}(L)\to X_{L} is not contained in YY.

Proof.

First assume L=kL=k. If YY is GG-invariant, the lemma follows from the definition of (T,K)(T,K)-versality. If YY is not GG-invariant, we proceed as follows. Let ZZ be the closure of the union ⋃im⁡(ψ)\bigcup\operatorname{im}(\psi), where ψ:T→X\psi:T\to X varies over all GG-equivariant kk-morphisms whose image is contained in YY. Since each ψ\psi is GG-equivariant, the closure of each im⁡(ψ)\operatorname{im}(\psi) is GG-invariant, as is the closure of their union. In other words, the subvariety ZZ is GG-invariant. Note that Z⊆Y⊊XZ\subseteq Y\subsetneq X. Since XX is (T,K)(T,K)-versal, there is a kk-morphism ψ:T→X\psi:T\to X whose image is in the complement of ZZ. By the construction of ZZ, the image of any such map is not contained in YY. This completes the proof of the lemma in the case where k=Lk=L.

Now assume L/kL/k is arbitrary. Let X=U1∪⋯∪UmX=U_{1}\cup\dots\cup U_{m} be an open affine cover of XX defined over kk. (We do not assume that the UiU_{i} are GG-invariant.) The defining equations of YY in each UiU_{i} involve only a finite number of elements of LL. Let RR be the kk-subalgebra of LL generated by all these elements. Then YY is, in fact, defined over Spec⁡(R)\operatorname{Spec}(R). In other words, there exists a closed kk-subvariety Y0⊂XR=X×kSpec⁡(R)Y_{0}\subset X_{R}=X\times_{k}\operatorname{Spec}(R) such that Y=Y0×RLY=Y_{0}\times_{R}L.

Since Y≠XLY\neq X_{L}, clearly Y0≠XRY_{0}\neq X_{R}. Let π:XR=X×kSpec⁡(R)→X\pi:X_{R}=X\times_{k}\operatorname{Spec}(R)\to X be the natural projection and

C:={x∈X|π−1​(x)⊂Y0}.C:=\{x\in X\,|\,\pi^{-1}(x)\subset Y_{0}\}.

Since π\pi is an open map and CC is the complement of the image of the complement of Y0Y_{0}, CC is a closed subvariety of XX defined over kk and C≠XC\neq X (because Y0≠XRY_{0}\neq X_{R}). As we showed above, there is a GG-equivariant kk-morphism ψ:T→X\psi:T\to X whose image is not contained in CC. Then the image of ψ×kSpec⁡(R):T×Spec⁡(R)→XR\psi\times_{k}\operatorname{Spec}(R)\colon T\times\operatorname{Spec}(R)\to X_{R} is not contained in Y0Y_{0} and thus, the image of ψL:T×Spec⁡(L)→XL\psi_{L}\colon T\times\operatorname{Spec}(L)\to X_{L} is not contained in YY. ∎

Corollary 4.5.

Let XX be a geometrically irreducible kk-variety, and let L/kL/k be a field extension. Note that there is a natural inclusion of sets X​(k)↪XL​(L)X(k)\hookrightarrow X_{L}(L) by pulling back Spec⁡(k)→X\operatorname{Spec}(k)\to X by Spec⁡(L)→Spec⁡(k)\operatorname{Spec}(L)\to\operatorname{Spec}(k). Then X⁡(k)X(k) is dense in XX if and only if X⁡(k)X(k) is dense in XLX_{L}.

Proof.

If LL is finite then the result is immediate: in this case X⁡(k)X(k) is dense in XX if and only if X⁡(k)X(k) is dense in X⁡(L)X(L) if and only if XX is a point. Thus we may assume that LL is infinite. The morphism XL→XX_{L}\to X is dominant, so one direction is obvious. The other implication is a special case of Lemma 4.4 with K=LK=L, G={1}G=\{1\} and T=Spec⁡(K)T=\operatorname{Spec}(K). ∎

Lemma 4.6.

Let X/kX/k be a geometrically irreducible GG-variety, let (T,K)(T,K) be a twisting pair, and let L/KL/K be a field extension which splits TT. Fix an LL-point s∈T⁡(L)s\in T(L). Then the following are equivalent:

  1. (a)

    (TX)(K)(^{T}X)(K) is dense in XT{}^{T}X,

  2. (b)

    the set of points fL​(s)f_{L}(s), where ff varies over all GG-equivariant kk-morphisms f:T→Xf\colon T\to X, is dense in XLX_{L}.

Note that condition (b) is considerably stronger than the condition that the union of fL​(T)f_{L}(T) is dense in XLX_{L}, which came up in Lemma 4.4. This discrepancy is precisely the source of the difficulty we encountered in Example 4.2.

Proof.

Since XX is geometrically irreducible, so is XT{}^{T}X. By Corollary 4.5, condition (a) is equivalent to

  1. (c)

    (TX)(K)(^{T}X)(K) is dense in (XT)L({}^{T}X)_{L}.

Let tst_{s} be an LL-isomorphism between (TX)L(\,^{T}X)_{L} and XLX_{L}, chosen so that

(s,ts):(TX)L→TL×XL(s,t_{s})\colon\,(^{T}X)_{L}\to T_{L}\times X_{L}

is a section (defined over LL) of the GG-torsor T×X→TXT\times X\to\,^{T}X, as in the statement of Corollary 3.3. Then (c) is equivalent to

  1. (d)

    the set of LL-points of the form ts​(q)t_{s}(q), where qq varies over (TX)(K)(^{T}X)(K), is dense in XLX_{L}.

By Corollary 3.3, (d) is equivalent to (b). ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.1(b).

⟸\impliedby (cf. [FF08, Proposition 1.12]): Assume KK-points are dense in XT{}^{T}X for every twisting pair (T,K)(T,K). We want to show that every dense GG-invariant open subvariety U⊂XU\subset X is weakly versal. By Theorem 1.1(a) it suffices to show that UT{}^{T}U contains a KK-point for every twisting pair (T,K)(T,K), as above. This follows from the fact that UT{}^{T}U is a dense open subvariety of XT{}^{T}X; see Corollary 3.4(b).

⟹\implies: Assume XX is versal. Then XX is geometrically irreducible; see Proposition 2.5. Fix a twisting pair (T,K)(T,K). We want to show KK-points are dense in XT{}^{T}X. Let LL be a splitting field for TT, and let ss be a point in T⁡(L)T(L). By Lemma 4.6, it suffices to show that for every closed subvariety Y⊊XLY\subsetneq X_{L} defined over LL, there exists a GG-equivariant kk-morphism f:T→Xf\colon T\to X such that fL​(s)∉Yf_{L}(s)\not\in Y.

As explained above, we cannot construct ff directly using only the fact that XX is (T,K)(T,K)-versal. We will instead construct ff in two steps, as a composition of a GG-equivariant kk-morphism f1:T→Vf_{1}\colon T\to V and a GG-equivariant rational map f2:V⇢Xf_{2}\colon V\dasharrow X. Here VV, SS and FF are as in Definition 4.3.

Let us begin by constructing f2f_{2}. Since XX is versal, by Lemma 4.4 there exists a GG-equivariant kk-morphism ψ:S→X\psi\colon S\to X such that the image of ψL\psi_{L} is not contained in YY. Equivalently, there exists a GG-equivariant rational kk-map f2:V⇢Xf_{2}\colon V\dasharrow X such that the image of (f2)L(f_{2})_{L} is not contained in YY. (Note that our construction of f2f_{2} makes use of the fact that XX is (S,F)(S,F)-versal, not just (T,K)(T,K)-versal.)

Let UU be a GG-invariant dense open subvariety of VV defined over kk, such that f2f_{2} is regular on UU. From now on f2f_{2} will denote the regular map U→XU\to X. Note that (f2)L−1​(Y)(f_{2})_{L}^{-1}(Y) is a closed subvariety of ULU_{L} and (f2)L−1​(Y)≠UL(f_{2})_{L}^{-1}(Y)\neq U_{L}. Now recall that by Lemma 3.1, KK-points are dense in VT≃VK{}^{T}V\simeq V_{K} and hence, in UT{}^{T}U. Thus, by Lemma 4.6, there exists a GG-equivariant kk-morphism f1:T→Uf_{1}\colon T\to U such that (f1)L​(s)∉(f2)L−1​(Y)(f_{1})_{L}(s)\not\in(f_{2})_{L}^{-1}(Y). By our construction, the composition f2​f1f_{2}f_{1} is a regular GG-equivariant morphism T→XT\to X and f2​f1​(s)∉Yf_{2}f_{1}(s)\not\in Y, as desired. This completes the proof of Theorem 1.1(b). ∎

Let XX, YY be geometrically irreducible kk-varieties and suppose XX has a GG-action. Proof of Theorem 1.1(c).

⟹\implies: Suppose XX is very versal, i.e., there exists a dominant GG-equivariant map f:W⇢Xf\colon W\dasharrow X. Then for any twisting pair (T,K)(T,K), the KK-rational map Tf:TW⇢TX\,{}^{T}f\colon\,^{T}W\dasharrow\,^{T}X is dominant; see Corollary 3.4. By Lemma 3.1, TW≃KWK{}^{T}W\simeq_{K}W_{K}. Thus XT{}^{T}X is KK-unirational.

⟸\impliedby: By assumption, there exists a dominant rational map 𝔸Fn⇢XS{\mathbb{A}}_{F}^{n}\dasharrow{}^{S}X for some integer nn. By Lemma 5.1, we obtain a dominant rational GG-equivariant kk-map V×𝔸kn⇢V×XV\times{\mathbb{A}}_{k}^{n}\dasharrow V\times X, where GG acts trivially on 𝔸kn{\mathbb{A}}_{k}^{n}. Composing this map with the projection V×X→XV\times X\to X, we see that XX is very versal. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.1(d).

⟹\implies: Suppose the GG-action on XX is stably birationally linear, i.e., there exists a GG-equivariant birational isomorphism ϕ:X×W1⇢≃W0\phi\colon X\times W_{1}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\dasharrow}}W_{0} for some linear representations G→GL⁡(W1)G\to\operatorname{GL}(W_{1}) and G→GL⁡(W0)G\to\operatorname{GL}(W_{0}) defined over kk. Twisting ϕ\phi by a twisting pair (T,K)(T,K), we obtain a birational isomorphism

ϕT:(TX)×K(TW1)⇢≃W0T.{}^{T}\phi\colon(^{T}X)\times_{K}(^{T}W_{1})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\dasharrow}}{}^{T}W_{0}\,.

Since W1T{}^{T}W_{1} and W0T{}^{T}W_{0} are affine spaces over KK (cf. Lemma 3.1), this tells us that XT{}^{T}X is stably rational over KK.

⟸\impliedby: By assumption, there is a birational isomorphism 𝔸Fn⇢≃XS×𝔸Fm{\mathbb{A}}_{F}^{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\dasharrow}}{}^{S}X\times{\mathbb{A}}_{F}^{m} defined over FF. Now note that XS×𝔸Fm≃(X×𝔸km)S{}^{S}X\times{\mathbb{A}}_{F}^{m}\simeq{}^{S}(X\times{\mathbb{A}}_{k}^{m}), where GG acts trivially on 𝔸km{\mathbb{A}}_{k}^{m}; cf. Corollary 3.4(a). By Lemma 5.1, we obtain a GG-equivariant birational isomorphism V×𝔸kn⇢≃V×X×𝔸kmV\times{\mathbb{A}}_{k}^{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\dasharrow}}V\times X\times{\mathbb{A}}_{k}^{m}, defined over kk. Here GG acts trivially on both 𝔸kn{\mathbb{A}}_{k}^{n} and 𝔸km{\mathbb{A}}_{k}^{m}. This shows that the GG-action on XX is stably birationally linear. ∎

6. Forms of Moduli Spaces

Throughout this section, the base field kk will be assumed to be of characteristic 00 and M¯g,n\overline{M}_{g,n} will denote the moduli space of stable curves of genus gg with nn marked points viewed as a kk-variety. The symmetric group Sn\operatorname{S}_{n} acts on M¯g,n\overline{M}_{g,n} by permuting the nn marked points. If k=ℂk={\mathbb{C}}, A. Massarenti [Mass11] showed that Sn\operatorname{S}_{n} is, in fact, the full automorphism group of M¯g,n\overline{M}_{g,n} whenever 2​g+n⩾52g+n\geqslant 5. This extends earlier work of A. Bruno and M. Mella [BM10] in the case where g=0g=0. In other words, if 2​g+n⩾52g+n\geqslant 5 then the natural homomorphism

ι:Sn→Aut⁡(M¯g,n)\iota\colon\operatorname{S}_{n}\to\operatorname{Aut}(\overline{M}_{g,n})

is an isomorphism. Here we view Aut⁡(M¯g,n)\operatorname{Aut}(\overline{M}_{g,n}) as a group scheme over kk. (The automorphisms of a complete variety carries a natural structure of an algebraic group scheme; cf. [MO67]. A priori this group scheme is neither affine nor of finite type over kk.) By the Lefschetz principle ι\iota is an isomorphism for any algebraically closed base field kk of characteristic zero. In fact, the same is true if kk is not assumed to be algebraically closed; this can be seen by descent [EGA IV, Proposition 2.7.1], after passing to k¯\overline{k}.

Theorem 6.1.

Suppose K/kK/k is a field extension. Then

  1. (a)

    For n⩾5n\geqslant 5, every KK-form of M¯0,n\overline{M}_{0,n} is KK-unirational.

  2. (b)

    For 3⩽n⩽93\leqslant n\leqslant 9, every KK-form of M¯1,n\overline{M}_{1,n} is KK-unirational.

Proof.

Let g=0g=0 in part (a) and g=1g=1 in part (b). Then 2​g+n⩾52g+n\geqslant 5 and hence, Sn\operatorname{S}_{n} is the full automorphism group of M¯g,n\overline{M}_{g,n}, in both parts. Consequently, every KK-form of M¯g,n\overline{M}_{g,n}, over a field extension K/kK/k is isomorphic to XT{}^{T}X for some Sn\operatorname{S}_{n}-torsor T→Spec⁡(K)T\to\operatorname{Spec}(K). By Theorem 1.1(c) it suffices to show that the Sn\operatorname{S}_{n}-action on M¯g,n\overline{M}_{g,n} is very versal.

(a) Consider the following composition of dominant Sn\operatorname{S}_{n}-equivariant rational maps:

(𝔸2)n⇢(ℙ1)n⇢M¯0,n.({\mathbb{A}}^{2})^{n}\dasharrow(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{n}\dasharrow\overline{M}_{0,n}\,.

Here the first map is nn parallel applications of the natural projection 𝔸2∖{0}→ℙ1{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus\{0\}\to{\mathbb{P}}^{1}, and the second map takes an nn-tuple of distinct points on ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1} to its class in M¯0,n\overline{M}_{0,n}. The symmetric group Sn\operatorname{S}_{n} acts on the 2​n2n-dimensional affine space (𝔸2)n({\mathbb{A}}^{2})^{n} linearly, by permuting the nn factors of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}. This shows that the action of Sn\operatorname{S}_{n} on M¯g,n\overline{M}_{g,n} is very versal.

(b) It suffices to consider the case where n=9n=9. Indeed, the natural map M¯g,n+1⇢M¯g,n\overline{M}_{g,n+1}\dasharrow\overline{M}_{g,n} which “forgets” the last marked point, is Sn\operatorname{S}_{n}-equivariant and dominant for any n⩾0n\geqslant 0. Thus if the Sn+1\operatorname{S}_{n+1}-action on M¯g,n+1\overline{M}_{g,n+1} is very versal then so is the Sn\operatorname{S}_{n}-action on M¯g,n\overline{M}_{g,n}.

To show that the S9\operatorname{S}_{9}-action on M¯1,9\overline{M}_{1,9} is very versal, we consider the following composition of dominant S9\operatorname{S}_{9}-equivariant maps:

(𝔸3)9⇢(ℙ2)9⇢M¯1,9.({\mathbb{A}}^{3})^{9}\dasharrow({\mathbb{P}}^{2})^{9}\dasharrow\overline{M}_{1,9}\,.

Here the first map projects each 𝔸3∖{0}{\mathbb{A}}^{3}\setminus\{0\} to ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2}. The second map takes a 99-tuple of points p1,…,p9∈ℙ2p_{1},\dots,p_{9}\in\mathbb{P}^{2} to the point of M¯1,9\overline{M}_{1,9} represented by (C,p1,…,p9)(C,p_{1},\dots,p_{9}), where CC is the plane cubic curve passing through p1,…,p9p_{1},\dots,p_{9}. Note that CC is uniquely determined and non-singular for p1,…,p9p_{1},\dots,p_{9} in general position. ∎

Remark 6.2.

It is well known that M¯0,5\overline{M}_{0,5} is a Del Pezzo surface of degree 55 and that every Del Pezzo surface of degree 55 over a field K/kK/k is a KK-form of M¯0,5\overline{M}_{0,5}. Thus, for n=5n=5, we recover the theorem of H. P. F. Swinnerton-Dyer [SD72] about the existence of rational points on such surfaces (in characteristic 00 only). For alternative proofs of Swinnerton-Dyer’s theorem, see [SB92] and [Sko93].

Remark 6.3.

Over ℂ{\mathbb{C}}, M¯1,n\overline{M}_{1,n} itself is known to be rational if n⩽10n\leqslant 10 (see [Bel98] or [CF07, Section 2]) and non-unirational for n⩾11n\geqslant 11; see [CF07, p. 583].

Note also that by [Mass11, p. 2], Aut⁡(M¯1,2)≃𝔾m2\operatorname{Aut}(\overline{M}_{1,2})\simeq{\mathbb{G}}_{m}^{2}, is a 22-dimensional torus. By Hilbert’s Theorem 90, H1​(K,𝔾m2)={1}H^{1}(K,{\mathbb{G}}_{m}^{2})=\{1\}, i.e., every torsor T→Spec⁡(K)T\to\operatorname{Spec}(K) is split for every field extension K/ℂK/{\mathbb{C}}. Thus M¯1,2\overline{M}_{1,2} has no non-trivial twisted forms: M¯1,2T≃(M¯1,2)K{}^{T}\overline{M}_{1,2}\simeq(\overline{M}_{1,2})_{K}. Since M¯1,2\overline{M}_{1,2} is rational over ℂ{\mathbb{C}} (see [Mass11, Proposition 2.1] or the references above), we conclude that every KK-form of M¯1,2\overline{M}_{1,2} is rational over KK, for every field extension K/ℂK/{\mathbb{C}}.

Remark 6.4.

The conclusion of Theorem 6.1 fails for M¯0,4≃M¯1,1≃ℙ1\overline{M}_{0,4}\simeq\overline{M}_{1,1}\simeq{\mathbb{P}}^{1} (over k¯\bar{k}). Indeed, in general, a form of ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1} (a 11-dimensional Brauer-Severi variety) has no rational points.

Remark 6.5.

If g⩾23g\geqslant 23 then M¯g,0\overline{M}_{g,0} is not unirational, and hence, neither is M¯g,n\overline{M}_{g,n} for any n⩾1n\geqslant 1. For each g⩽22g\leqslant 22, A. Logan [Lo03] showed that there is an explicit function f⁡(g)f(g) such that M¯g,n\overline{M}_{g,n} is not unirational for any n⩾f⁡(g)n\geqslant f(g). Some (but not all) of the spaces M¯g,n\overline{M}_{g,n} with n<f⁡(g)n<f(g) have since been shown to be unirational; for details and further references, see [BCF09, Introduction]. Beyond the results of this section, we do not know which of the finitely many unirational spaces M¯g,n\overline{M}_{g,n} have the property that every form of M¯g,n\overline{M}_{g,n} over every K/kK/k is also unirational. In particular, we do not know if Theorem 6.1 remains valid for M¯1,10\overline{M}_{1,10}.

7. Homogeneous Spaces

Proposition 7.1.

Let AA be an algebraic group over kk. If Char⁡(k)>0\operatorname{Char}(k)>0, assume that AA is reductive. Suppose GG and BB are closed subgroups of AA, and X:=A/BX:=A/B is geometrically irreducible. Consider XX as a GG-variety. The following are equivalent:

  1. (a)

    XX is very versal,

  2. (b)

    XX is versal,

  3. (c)

    XX is weakly versal,

  4. (d)

    the image of the natural map H1​(K,G)→H1​(K,A)H^{1}(K,G)\to H^{1}(K,A) is contained in the image of the natural map H1​(K,B)→H1​(K,A)H^{1}(K,B)\to H^{1}(K,A) for every field extension K/kK/k where KK is infinite.

Proof.

Let (T,K)(T,K) be a twisting pair. In view of Proposition 3.6, XT{}^{T}X is a homogeneous space for the twisted group AT{}^{T}A.

By Theorem 1.1 it suffices to show that the following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    XT{}^{T}X has a KK-point,

  2. (ii)

    there exists a dominant AT{}^{T}A-equivariant map f:TA→TXf\colon\,^{T}A\to\,^{T}X defined over KK,

  3. (iii)

    XT{}^{T}X is KK-unirational,

  4. (iv)

    KK-points are dense in XT{}^{T}X,

  5. (v)

    the class of TT lies in the image of the natural map H1​(K,B)→H1​(K,A)H^{1}(K,B)\to H^{1}(K,A).

(i) ⟹\Longrightarrow (ii): By Proposition 3.6 AT\,{}^{T}A acts on XT{}^{T}X. If p∈X⁡(K)p\in X(K), we can define ff to be the orbit map f⁡(g)=g⋅pf(g)=g\cdot p. Passing to a splitting field of TT, we see that ff is dominant.

(ii) ⟹\Longrightarrow (iii): Let (AT)∘({}^{T}A)^{\circ} be the connected component of the identity in AT{}^{T}A. Note that the composition (AT)∘→AT→XT({}^{T}A)^{\circ}\to{}^{T}A\to{}^{T}X is also dominant since XT{}^{T}X is geometrically irreducible.

We use a theorem of Chevalley [Bor91, Theorem 18.2(ii)] which asserts that a connected linear algebraic group is unirational when either the group is reductive or the ground field is perfect. Thus, under our assumptions on AA, (AT)∘({}^{T}A)^{\circ} is unirational.

The implications (iii) ⟹\Longrightarrow (iv) ⟹\Longrightarrow (i) are obvious.

(ii) ⟺\Longleftrightarrow (v) is proved in [Ser02, Proposition I.5.37]; see also [Spr66, Proposition 1.11]. ∎

Remark 7.2.

Note that the above argument fails if Char⁡(k)>0\operatorname{Char}(k)>0 and we do not assume that AA is reductive, even if kk is a perfect field. Indeed, in this case Chevalley’s theorem tells us that the group A0A^{0} is unirational over kk. However, the twisted group (AT)∘({}^{T}A)^{\circ}, defined over an (a priori arbitrary) extension K/kK/k may not be unirational over KK, since KK may not be perfect.

Example 7.3.

We record several interesting special cases of Proposition 7.1 when AA is connected.

(a) Suppose B={1}B=\{1\}. Then the translation action of a subgroup GG on AA is versal if and only if the natural map H1​(K,G)→H1​(K,A)H^{1}(K,G)\to H^{1}(K,A) is trivial for every field extension K/kK/k, where KK is infinite. The same is true whenever BB is a special group, i.e., whenever H1​(K,B)H^{1}(K,B) is trivial for every K/kK/k.

(b) Setting B=GB=G yields the following: For any closed subgroup G⊂AG\subset A, the translation action of GG on A/GA/G is very versal.

(c) If BB is the normalizer of a maximal torus in AA, we see that the translation action of GG on A/BA/B is very versal for any G⊂AG\subset A. This is because the natural map H1​(K,B)→H1​(K,A)H^{1}(K,B)\to H^{1}(K,A) is surjective for every field extension K/kK/k; see [Ser02, III.4.3, Lemma 6] if KK is perfect and [CGR08, Corollary 5.3] otherwise.

We may also apply Chevalley’s theorem in cases where GG acts via group automorphisms rather than by translations.

Example 7.4.

(cf. [CTKPR11, Proposition 3.3]) Let HH be a connected algebraic group. If Char⁡(k)>0\operatorname{Char}(k)>0, assume that HH is reductive. Then every action of an algebraic group GG on HH by group automorphisms is very versal.

Proof.

Let (T,K)(T,K) be a twisting pair. By Proposition 3.5, HT{}^{T}H carries the structure of an affine algebraic group over KK. By Chevalley’s theorem [Bor91, Theorem 18.2(ii)] HT{}^{T}H is unirational over KK. The desired conclusion now follows from Theorem 1.1(c). ∎

8. pp-versality

Throughout this section, pp is a prime number.

Definition 8.1.

Let G/kG/k be an algebraic group and let X/kX/k be an irreducible GG-variety. We say that XX is

  • •

    weakly pp-versal if for every twisting pair (T,K)(T,K), there exists a field extension L/KL/K of degree prime to pp and a GG-equivariant kk-morphism TL→XT_{L}\to X,

  • •

    pp-versal if every GG-invariant dense open subvariety U⊂XU\subset X is weakly pp-versal (cf. [Mer09, Section 2.2]).

Recall that a field LL is called pp-closed if the degree of every finite field extension of LL is a power of pp. For every field KK, there exists an algebraic extension K(p)/KK^{(p)}/K, such that K(p)K^{(p)} is pp-closed and, for every finite subextension K⊂K′⊂K(p)K\subset K^{\prime}\subset K^{(p)}, the degree [K′:K][K^{\prime}:K] is prime to pp. The field K(p)K^{(p)} satisfying these conditions is unique up to KK-isomorphism; it usually called the pp-closure of KK and is denoted by K(p)K^{(p)}. For details, see [EKM08, Proposition 101.16].

Lemma 8.2.

Let XX be a geometrically irreducible GG-variety defined over kk. Then the following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (a)

    XX is weakly pp-versal,

  2. (b)

    for every twisting pair (T,K)(T,K), XT{}^{T}X has a point whose degree over KK is prime to pp,

  3. (c)

    for every twisting pair (T,K)(T,K), XT{}^{T}X has a 00-cycle whose degree is prime to pp,

  4. (d)

    for every twisting pair (T,K)(T,K), the variety (TX)K(p)(^{T}X)_{K^{(p)}} has a 00-cycle of degree 11,

  5. (e)

    for every twisting pair (T,K)(T,K), the variety XT{}^{T}X has a K(p)K^{(p)}-point.

Proof.

(a) ⟺\Longleftrightarrow (b): By Proposition 3.2, the existence of an LL-point of XT{}^{T}X is equivalent to the existence of a GG-equivariant kk-morphism TL→XT_{L}\to X.

(b) ⟹\implies (c) is obvious.

(c) ⟹\implies (d): Suppose Z⊂XTZ\subset{}^{T}X is a 00-cycle of degree dd, where dd is prime to pp. Since the degree of every closed point of (TX)K(p)(^{T}X)_{K^{(p)}} is a power of pp, there exists a 00-cycle Z′⊂(TX)K(p)Z^{\prime}\subset(^{T}X)_{K^{(p)}} whose degree is a power of pp. A desired 00-cycle of degree 11 on (TX)K(p)(^{T}X)_{K^{(p)}} can then be constructed as an integer linear combination of ZZ and Z′Z^{\prime}.

(d) ⟹\implies (e): (cf. [Ful85, Example 13.1]) This is immediate from the fact that the degree of every closed point on (TX)K(p)(^{T}X)_{K^{(p)}} is a power of pp.

(e) ⟹\implies (b): Every K(p)K^{(p)}-point of XT{}^{T}X descends to a finitely generated subextension K⊂L⊂K(p)K\subset L\subset K^{(p)}. The field LL is then a finite extension of KK whose degree is prime to pp. ∎

Theorem 8.3.

Let GG be an algebraic group acting on a smooth geometrically irreducible kk-variety XX. Then XX is pp-versal if and only if XX is weakly pp-versal.

Proof.

We will assume that XX is weakly pp-versal and prove that XX is pp-versal; the other direction is obvious.

Let U⊂XU\subset X be a GG-invariant dense open subvariety. We want to show that UU is weakly versal. Let (T,K)(T,K) be a twisting pair. By Lemma 8.2, it suffices to prove that if XT{}^{T}X has a 00-cycle whose degree is prime to pp, then so does UT{}^{T}U. Since UT{}^{T}U is a dense open subvariety of XT{}^{T}X (see Corollary 3.4(b)), this is a special case of Chow’s Moving Lemma [Ful85, Section 11.4]. ∎

Remark 8.4.

The above argument only requires Chow’s Moving Lemma for 00-cycles. This special case of the Moving Lemma is quite elementary: to prove it, one constructs a smooth curve passing through a given 00-cycle, then moves the 00-cycle along this curve.

Remark 8.5.

We thank an anonymous referee for pointing out that Theorem 8.3 is closely related to the fact that every pp-closed field LL is “ample” (or “large”). That is, if an irreducible LL-variety has a smooth LL-point, then the LL-points are Zariski dense. This property of pp-closed fields was noticed by J.-L. Colliot-Thélène [CT00] in the case where LL is perfect. In the case where LL is not perfect it was proved by M. Jarden [Jar03].

Corollary 8.6.

Let X/kX/k be a geometrically irreducible generically smooth GG-variety.

  1. (a)

    Assume that GG has a closed subgroup HH whose index is finite and prime to pp. Then the GG-action on XX is pp-versal if and only if the restricted HH-action is pp-versal.

  2. (b)

    Suppose there exists a smooth kk-point x∈X⁡(k)x\in X(k) such that the orbit G⋅xG\cdot x is finite and deg⁡([G⋅x])\deg([G\cdot x]) is prime to pp. Then the GG-action on XX is pp-versal.

Proof.

After replacing XX by its smooth locus, we may assume that XX is smooth.

(a) From the proof of [MR09, Lemma 4.1], for any field K/kK/k, the map H1​(K,H)→H1​(K,G)H^{1}(K,H)\to H^{1}(K,G) is pp-surjective. That is, for any α∈H1​(K,G)\alpha\in H^{1}(K,G) there exists a finite extension L/KL/K of degree prime to pp such that αL\alpha_{L} lies in the image of the natural map H1​(L,H)→H1​(L,G)H^{1}(L,H)\to H^{1}(L,G). If KK is pp-closed, then [L:K][L:K] is a power of pp, so L=KL=K, and the map H1​(K,H)→H1​(K,G)H^{1}(K,H)\to H^{1}(K,G) is surjective. In other words, for any HH-torsor T→Spec⁡(K)T\to\operatorname{Spec}(K), there exists a GG-torsor T′→Spec⁡(K)T^{\prime}\to\operatorname{Spec}(K) such that XT{}^{T}X and XT′{}^{T^{\prime}}X become isomorphic over K(p)K^{(p)}. In particular, XT{}^{T}X has a K(p)K^{(p)}-point if and only if XT′{}^{T^{\prime}}X has a K(p)K^{(p)}-point. Lemma 8.2 now tells us that the GG-action on XX is weakly pp-versal if and only the HH-action is weakly pp-versal. By Theorem 8.3, the same is true if “weakly pp-versal” is replaced by “pp-versal”.

(b) Let HH be the stabilizer of xx in GG. Then xx is fixed by HH, and the index [G:H]=deg([G⋅x])[G:H]=\deg([G\cdot x]) is finite and prime to pp. By Proposition 2.2, the HH-action on XX is weakly versal. By Theorem 8.3, the HH-action on XX is pp-versal. By part (a) the GG-action on XX is pp-versal as well. ∎

We also note the following immediate consequence of Theorem 8.3 and Lemma 8.2, in the spirit of Theorem 1.1.

Corollary 8.7.

A GG-action on a smooth geometrically irreducible variety XX is pp-versal for every prime pp if and only if, for every twisting pair (T,K)(T,K), XT{}^{T}X has a 00-cycle of degree 11. ∎

Every versal GG-variety is clearly pp-versal for every prime pp. However, the converse is not true in general, even if G={1}G=\{1\}; after all, there exist kk-varieties with 00-cycles of degree 11 but no kk-points. On the other hand, no counterexample is known for the following weaker statement:

Conjecture 8.8 (cf. [Dun09]).

Let GG be a finite constant group, XX be a GG-variety and GpG_{p} be a Sylow pp-subgroup of GG. If XX is GpG_{p}-versal for every prime pp, then XX is GG-versal.

Note that the key assumption here is that XX is versal and not just pp-versal as a GpG_{p}-variety.

Remark 8.9.

It is natural to define a GG-variety XX to be “very pp-versal” if there exists a linear representation VV, and a diagram of dominant rational GG-equivariant maps of the form

where the degree of V′⇢VV^{\prime}\dasharrow V is prime to pp. (Note that V′V^{\prime} is not required to be a vector space.) Under mild assumptions on XX this notion also turns out to be equivalent to pp-versality.

9. Projective representations

Let GG be a finite subgroup of PGLn\operatorname{PGL}_{n} defined over kk and G′G^{\prime} be the preimage of GG in GLn\operatorname{GL}_{n}. The diagram

(9.1)

gives rise to the connecting morphism ∂K:H1​(K,G)→H2​(K,𝔾m)\partial_{K}:H^{1}(K,G)\to H^{2}(K,\mathbb{G}_{m}) for every field K/kK/k.

Proposition 9.1.

(cf. [Dun09, Corollary 3.4]) Let GG be a finite subgroup of PGLn\operatorname{PGL}_{n} defined over kk. Then the following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (a)

    The GG-action on ℙn−1{\mathbb{P}}^{n-1} is stably birationally linear,

  2. (b)

    the GG-action on ℙn−1{\mathbb{P}}^{n-1} is very versal,

  3. (c)

    the GG-action on ℙn−1{\mathbb{P}}^{n-1} is versal,

  4. (d)

    the GG-action on ℙn−1{\mathbb{P}}^{n-1} is weakly versal,

  5. (e)

    the GG-action on ℙn−1{\mathbb{P}}^{n-1} is pp-versal for every prime pp,

  6. (f)

    ∂K=0\partial_{K}=0 for every K/kK/k,

  7. (g)

    GG lifts to a subgroup of GLn\operatorname{GL}_{n}, i.e., the exact sequence (9.1) splits.

Proof.

Let (T,K)(T,K) be a GG-twisting pair. Then X=T(ℙn−1)X=\,^{T}({\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}) is a Brauer-Severi variety over KK whose class is ∂K([T])\partial_{K}([T]), where [T][T] is the class of TT in H1​(K,G)H^{1}(K,G). It is well known that a Brauer-Severi variety XX over KK is KK-rational if and only if XX has a 00-cycle of degree 11 if and only if the class of XX in H2​(K,𝔾m)H^{2}(K,\mathbb{G}_{m}) is trivial. This shows that conditions (a) - (f) are all equivalent by Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 8.7.

(g) ⟹\Longrightarrow (b). If GG lifts to GLn\operatorname{GL}_{n} then the natural projection map 𝔸n∖{0}→ℙn−1\mathbb{A}^{n}\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb{P}^{n-1} is dominant and GG-equivariant, and (b) follows.

(f) ⟹\Longrightarrow (g). By [KM08, Theorem 4.4 and Remark 4.5], (f) implies

gcd⁡dimρ⁡(ρ)=1,\gcd_{\rho}\,\dim(\rho)=1\,,

as ρ\rho ranges over representations G′→GL⁡(V)G^{\prime}\to\operatorname{GL}(V) such that ρ⁡(t)=t​IV\rho(t)=t\operatorname{I}_{V} for every t∈𝔾mt\in\mathbb{G}_{m}. Here IVI_{V} is the identity map on VV. Thus there exist representations ρ1,…,ρm\rho_{1},\dots,\rho_{m} of GG and integers d1,…,dmd_{1},\dots,d_{m} such that the multiplicative character χ=det(ρ1)d1​…​det(ρm)dm:G′→𝔾m\chi=\det(\rho_{1})^{d_{1}}\dots\det(\rho_{m})^{d_{m}}\colon G^{\prime}\to{\mathbb{G}}_{m} has the property that χ⁡(t)=t\chi(t)=t and hence splits the sequence (9.1) (Ker⁡(χ)\operatorname{Ker}(\chi) is a complement of 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m} in G′G^{\prime}). ∎

10. Group actions on quadric and cubic hypersurfaces

Lemma 10.1.

Let VV be a finite-dimensional kk-vector space, G→GL⁡(V)G\to\operatorname{GL}(V) be a linear representation and XX be a closed GG-invariant subvariety of ℙ⁡(V){\mathbb{P}}(V).

  1. (a)

    For any twisting pair (T,K)(T,K), ℙT​(V){}^{T}{\mathbb{P}}(V) is KK-isomorphic to ℙ​(V)K{\mathbb{P}}(V)_{K}.

  2. (b)

    The inclusion ι:X↪ℙ⁡(V)\iota\colon X\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}(V) induces a closed embedding ιT:XT↪ℙ​(V)K{}^{T}\iota\colon{}^{T}X\hookrightarrow\,{\mathbb{P}}(V)_{K} with the same Hilbert polynomial as XX.

  3. (c)

    If d:=deg⁡(X)d:=\deg(X) is prime to pp then XX is pp-versal.

Proof.

(a) By Lemma 3.1, VT≃VK{}^{T}V\simeq V_{K}. The (T,K)(T,K)-twist of the natural projection V⇢ℙ⁡(V)V\dasharrow\mathbb{P}(V), is thus a dominant rational map VK⇢ℙT​(V)V_{K}\dasharrow{}^{T}{\mathbb{P}}(V). Consequently, the Brauer-Severi variety ℙT​(V){}^{T}{\mathbb{P}}(V) has a KK-point, and part (a) follows.

(b) Since the embeddings ιT:XT→ℙ​(V)K{}^{T}\iota:{}^{T}X\to{\mathbb{P}}(V)_{K} and ι:X→ℙ⁡(V)\iota:X\to{\mathbb{P}}(V) become projectively equivalent over an algebraic closure K¯\bar{K}, they have the same Hilbert polynomial.

(c) By part (b), XT{}^{T}X is a closed subvariety of ℙ⁡(VK)\mathbb{P}(V_{K}) of degree dd, defined over KK. Intersecting XT{}^{T}X with a suitable linear subvariety of ℙ⁡(VK){\mathbb{P}}(V_{K}) of complementary dimension, we obtain a smooth 00-cycle of degree dd on XT{}^{T}X defined over KK. Since dd is not divisible by pp, Lemma 8.2 and Theorem 8.3 now tell us that XX is pp-versal. ∎

Theorem 10.2.

Let GG be an algebraic group over kk, G→GL⁡(V)G\to\operatorname{GL}(V) be a finite-dimensional linear representation over kk, and X⊂ℙ⁡(V)X\subset{\mathbb{P}}(V) be a smooth GG-invariant quadratic hypersurface. Assume dim(V)⩾3\dim(V)\geqslant 3. The following are equivalent:

  1. (a)

    XX is stably birationally linear,

  2. (b)

    XX is very versal,

  3. (c)

    XX is versal,

  4. (d)

    XX is weakly versal,

  5. (e)

    XX is 22-versal.

Assume further that GG is finite, and G2G_{2} is a Sylow 22-subgroup of GG. Then conditions (a) – (e) are equivalent to

  1. (f)

    XX is versal for the action of G2G_{2}.

Proof.

Let (T,K)(T,K) be a twisting pair. By Lemma 10.1, Q:=XTQ:={}^{T}X is an irreducible quadratic hypersurface in ℙKn{\mathbb{P}}^{n}_{K} defined over KK. The equivalence of conditions (a)–(d) now follows from Theorem 1.1 and the following well-known property of irreducible quadric hypersurfaces Q⊂ℙ​(V)KQ\subset\mathbb{P}(V)_{K}:

(10.1) if QQ has a smooth KK-point then XX is KK-rational.

The equivalence of (a) and (e) is an immediate consequence of Springer’s theorem: if QQ has a smooth LL-point for some odd degree extension L/KL/K then QQ has a smooth KK-point.

If GG is a finite group then (f) ⟹\implies (e) by Corollary 8.6(a). On the other hand, (b) ⟹\implies XX is very versal as a G2G_{2}-variety ⟹\implies (f). ∎

If we replace a quadric hypersurface by a cubic hypersurface of dimension ⩾2\geqslant 2 then property (10.1) in the proof of Theorem 10.2 remains true, provided that “rational” is replaced by “unirational”, and Springer’s Theorem becomes an open conjecture. The precise statements are as follows.

Theorem 10.3.

([Kol02]) Let X⊂ℙknX\subset{\mathbb{P}}^{n}_{k} be a smooth cubic hypersurface where n⩾3n\geqslant 3. If XX has a kk-point then XX is kk-unirational.

Conjecture 10.4 (J. W. S. Cassels, P. Swinnerton-Dyer; see [Cor76]).

Suppose X⊂ℙknX\subset{\mathbb{P}}^{n}_{k} is a cubic hypersurface. If XX has a 00-cycle of degree prime to 33, then XX has a kk-point.

The argument we used to prove Theorem 10.2 now yields the following analogous statement for cubic hypersurfaces.

Theorem 10.5.

Let GG be an algebraic group over kk, G→GL⁡(V)G\to\operatorname{GL}(V) be a finite-dimensional linear representation over kk and X⊂ℙ⁡(V)X\subset{\mathbb{P}}(V) be a smooth GG-invariant cubic hypersurface. Assume dim(V)⩾4\dim(V)\geqslant 4. The following are equivalent:

  1. (a)

    XX is very versal,

  2. (b)

    XX is versal,

  3. (c)

    XX is weakly versal.

Now suppose GG is finite, G3G_{3} is a Sylow 33-subgroup of GG, and Conjecture 10.4 holds. Then (a) ⇔\Leftrightarrow (b) ⇔\Leftrightarrow (c) ⇔\Leftrightarrow (d) ⇔\Leftrightarrow (e), where

  1. (d)

    XX is 33-versal,

  2. (e)

    XX is versal for the action of G3G_{3}. ∎

Note that Conjecture 10.4 is known to be true only for n=2n=2; see, e.g., [Cor76]. In the statement of Theorem 10.5 we are assuming that n=dim(V)−1⩾3n=\dim(V)-1\geqslant 3.

Corollary 10.6.

Suppose an algebraic group GG acts on a smooth cubic hypersurface XX as in Theorem 10.5. If GG fixes a kk-point x∈X⁡(k)x\in X(k) then XX is GG-versal.

Proof.

By Proposition 2.2 the GG-action on XX is weakly versal. Theorem 10.5 now tells us that this action is versal. ∎

We now recall the definitions of two important numerical invariants of a finite group GG. The essential dimension, ed⁡(G)\operatorname{ed}(G) of GG is the minimal dimension of a versal GG-variety with a faithful GG-action; see [BR97], [R10] or Remark 2.6. The Cremona dimension, Crdim⁡(G)\operatorname{Crdim}(G) is the minimal integer nn such that GG embeds into the Cremona group Cr⁡(n)\operatorname{Cr}(n) of birational automorphisms of the affine space 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n}.

For the rest of this section we will assume that the base field kk is the field ℂ\mathbb{C} of complex numbers.

Conjecture 10.7.

(I. Dolgachev, unpublished) ed⁡(G)⩾Crdim⁡(G)\operatorname{ed}(G)\geqslant\operatorname{Crdim}(G) for every finite group GG.

Proposition 10.8.
  1. (a)

    Conjecture 8.8 implies ed⁡(PSL2⁡(𝔽11))=3\operatorname{ed}(\operatorname{PSL}_{2}({\mathbb{F}}_{11}))=3.

  2. (b)

    Conjecture 10.4 implies ed⁡(PSL2⁡(𝔽11))=3\operatorname{ed}(\operatorname{PSL}_{2}({\mathbb{F}}_{11}))=3.

  3. (c)

    Conjecture 10.7 implies ed⁡(PSL2⁡(𝔽11))=4\operatorname{ed}(\operatorname{PSL}_{2}({\mathbb{F}}_{11}))=4.

Proof.

Consider the Klein cubic, i.e., the smooth cubic threefold X⊂ℙ4X\subset{\mathbb{P}}^{4} cut out by

x02​x1+x12​x2+x22​x3+x32​x4+x42​x0=0.x_{0}^{2}x_{1}+x_{1}^{2}x_{2}+x_{2}^{2}x_{3}+x_{3}^{2}x_{4}+x_{4}^{2}x_{0}=0\,.

The automorphism group of XX is G=PSL2⁡(𝔽11)G=\operatorname{PSL}_{2}({\mathbb{F}}_{11}). The action of this group on XX is induced by a linear representation ϕ:G→GL5\phi\colon G\to\operatorname{GL}_{5} [Adl78].

It is easy to see that 3⩽ed⁡(PSL2⁡(𝔽11))⩽43\leqslant\operatorname{ed}(\operatorname{PSL}_{2}({\mathbb{F}}_{11}))\leqslant 4. Indeed, since GG is simple, the projection map ℂ5∖{0}→ℙ4{\mathbb{C}}^{5}\setminus\{0\}\to{\mathbb{P}}^{4} shows that the GG-action on ℙ4{\mathbb{P}}^{4} is generically free and very versal; hence, ed⁡(PSL2⁡(𝔽11))⩽4\operatorname{ed}(\operatorname{PSL}_{2}({\mathbb{F}}_{11}))\leqslant 4. The lower bound, 3⩽ed⁡(PSL2⁡(𝔽11))3\leqslant\operatorname{ed}(\operatorname{PSL}_{2}({\mathbb{F}}_{11})), follows from the fact that PSL2⁡(𝔽11)\operatorname{PSL}_{2}({\mathbb{F}}_{11}) cannot act faithfully on a unirational surface; see [Pro12, Dun09].

Since ϕ\phi is irreducible, no point of XX can be fixed by GG. However, from [Bea11] we see that XX has a GpG_{p}-fixed point for any Sylow pp-subgroup GpG_{p} of GG. Hence, by Corollary 10.6, the GpG_{p}-action on XX is versal for every prime pp. Now

(a) Conjecture 8.8 implies that XX is GG-versal. Thus ed⁡(G)⩽dim(X)⩽3\operatorname{ed}(G)\leqslant\dim(X)\leqslant 3.

(b) Conjecture 10.4 also implies that the GG-action on XX is versal; see Theorem 10.5. Consequently, ed⁡(G)⩽3\operatorname{ed}(G)\leqslant 3, as in part (a).

(c) From work of Yu. Prokhorov [Pro12, Theorem 1.3], we see that there are no rational complex threefolds with a faithful action of PSL2⁡(𝔽11)\operatorname{PSL}_{2}({\mathbb{F}}_{11}). This means that Crdim⁡(PSL2⁡(𝔽11))⩾4\operatorname{Crdim}(\operatorname{PSL}_{2}({\mathbb{F}}_{11}))\geqslant 4, and part (c) follows. ∎

We conclude that Conjectures 10.4 and 10.7 are incompatible; they cannot both be true. Same for Conjectures 8.8 and  10.7.

Remark 10.9.

If we knew whether ed⁡(PSL2⁡(𝔽11))\operatorname{ed}(\operatorname{PSL}_{2}({\mathbb{F}}_{11})) is 33 or 44, we would be able to complete the classification of finite simple groups of essential dimension 33 over ℂ{\mathbb{C}}. For details, see [Bea11].

Remark 10.10.

By [Pro12, Theorem 1.5], there are only two equivariant birational equivalence classes of rationally connected complex PSL2⁡(𝔽11)\operatorname{PSL}_{2}({\mathbb{F}}_{11})-threefolds, represented by the Klein cubic and a Fano threefold of genus 88. These threefolds are (non-equivariantly) birationally equivalent [Pro12, Remark 2.10]. They are unirational (cf. Theorem 10.3) but not rational [CG72].

Remark 10.11.

We are grateful to an anonymous referee for pointing out that Theorem 10.2 remains valid for an arbitrary GG-action on XX, even if we do not assume that this action comes from a linear representation G→GL⁡(V)G\to\operatorname{GL}(V). Indeed, suppose X⊂ℙ⁡(V)X\subset{\mathbb{P}}(V) is the zero locus of a non-degenerate quadratic form qq in VV. By [EKM08, Corollary 69.6] the natural inclusion PGO⁡(q)↪Aut⁡(X)\operatorname{PGO}(q)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Aut}(X) is an isomorphism. Thus the action of GG on XX gives rise to a morphism ψ:G→PGO⁡(q)\psi\colon G\to\operatorname{PGO}(q), which fits into the diagram

(10.2)

where G′G^{\prime} is the pull-back G×PGO⁡(q)GO⁡(q)G\times_{\operatorname{PGO}(q)}\operatorname{GO}(q). Denote the connecting morphism H1​(K,PGO⁡(q))→H2​(K,𝔾m)H^{1}(K,\operatorname{PGO}(q))\to H^{2}(K,{\mathbb{G}}_{m}) associated to the bottom sequence in (10.2) by ∂K\partial_{K}. The connecting homomorphism for the top sequence is then given by the composition

∂KG:H1​(K,G)→ψ∗H1​(K,PGO⁡(q))→∂KH2​(K,𝔾m),\partial_{K}^{G}\colon H^{1}(K,G)\xrightarrow{\psi_{*}}H^{1}(K,\operatorname{PGO}(q))\xrightarrow{\partial_{K}}H^{2}(K,{\mathbb{G}}_{m})\,,

Now suppose (T,K)(T,K) is a twisting pair for GG. Then XT⊂ℙT​(V){}^{T}X\subset{}^{T}\mathbb{P}(V), where ℙT​(V){}^{T}\mathbb{P}(V) is a Brauer-Severi variety over KK whose class is ∂KG[T]\partial_{K}^{G}\,[T]. Here [T][T] is the class of TT in H1​(K,G)H^{1}(K,G) as in the proof of Proposition 9.1

We claim that, for any α∈H1​(K,PGO⁡(q))\alpha\in H^{1}(K,\operatorname{PGO}(q)), the exponent of ∂(α)∈H2​(K,𝔾m)\partial(\alpha)\in H^{2}(K,{\mathbb{G}}_{m}) is 11 or 22. Let us assume this claim for now. Taking α=ψ∗​[T]\alpha=\psi_{*}\,[T], we see that the exponent of ∂KG[T]\partial_{K}^{G}\,[T] is 11 or 22. Hence, the index of this class (or equivalently, the index of the Brauer-Severi variety ℙT​(V){}^{T}\mathbb{P}(V)), is a power of 22. If any of the conditions (a) - (f) of Theorem 10.2 hold, then XT{}^{T}X (and thus ℙT​(V){}^{T}\mathbb{P}(V)) has a point or a 00-cycle of odd degree over KK. Hence, ℙT​(V){}^{T}\mathbb{P}(V) is split. Equivalently, ∂KG[T]=0\partial_{K}^{G}\,[T]=0. Since this is true for every T∈H1​(K,G)T\in H^{1}(K,G) and every K/kK/k, Proposition 9.1 tells us that the top sequence in (10.2) splits. Thus ψ:G→PGO⁡(q)\psi\colon G\to\operatorname{PGO}(q) lifts to a linear representation G→GO⁡(q)⊂GL⁡(V)G\to\operatorname{GO}(q)\subset\operatorname{GL}(V), and we find ourselves in the setting of Theorem 10.2.

It remains to prove the claim. Let n=dim(V)n=\dim(V). If nn is odd, then by [KMRT98, Propositions 12.4 and 12.6] the bottom short exact sequence in (10.2) splits. Hence, in this case ∂K=0\partial_{K}=0. In other words, the exponent of ∂K(α)\partial_{K}(\alpha) is 11 for every α∈H1​(K,PGO⁡(q))\alpha\in H^{1}(K,\operatorname{PGO}(q)).

Now assume that nn is even. In this case classes α∈H1​(K,PGO⁡(q))\alpha\in H^{1}(K,\operatorname{PGO}(q)) are in natural bijection with isomorphism classes of triples (A,σ,f)(A,\sigma,f), where AA is a central simple algebra of degree nn and (σ,f)(\sigma,f) is a quadratic pair on AA; see [KMRT98, p. 409]. The connecting map ∂K\partial_{K} takes α\alpha to the Brauer class [A]∈H2​(K,𝔾m)[A]\in H^{2}(K,{\mathbb{G}}_{m}). By [KMRT98, Definition (5.4)], σ\sigma is an involution of the first kind on AA. (Note that if Char⁡(K)≠2\operatorname{Char}(K)\neq 2 then σ\sigma is orthogonal and ff is uniquely determined by σ\sigma. In other words, in this case a quadratic pair on AA is the same thing as an orthogonal involution.) By a theorem of Albert (see, e.g., [KMRT98, Theorem (3.1)]), since AA has an involution of the first kind, the exponent of ∂K(α)=[A]\partial_{K}(\alpha)=[A] is 11 or 22. This proves the claim.

Remark 10.12.

Combining the argument of Remark 10.11 with Lemma 10.1(c), we see that any action of an algebraic group GG on a smooth irreducible quadric hypersurface X⊂ℙnX\subset\mathbb{P}^{n} is pp-versal, for every odd prime pp.

Appendix: Letter from J.-P. Serre to Z. Reichstein

Paris, June 10, 2010

Dear Reichstein,

About “versal” :

There was first the notion of a “universal object”, a notion which appeared in several branches of mathematics around 1930–1950; there is even a section of Bourbaki’s Théorie des Ensembles (chap.IV, §\lx@sectionsign2) on the general properties of this notion. An especially interesting case being the universal GG-principal homogeneous space (now “GG-torsor”); the case of G=GL⁡(n)G=\operatorname{GL}(n) was basically due to Chern. Such spaces (EG→BGE_{G}\to B_{G} was the standard notation) were very useful to topologists; see e.g. Borel’s thesis.

In the definition of “universal”, there is a uniqueness property (up to homotopy, sometimes) which is required. There are many interesting cases where it does not hold (e.g. deformations of complex manifolds, à la Kodaira- Spencer); people called them “almost universal” (or quasi , or semi …\ldots). I do not know exactly when somebody had the amusing idea to call them ‘‘versal’’, by deleting the ‘‘uni’’ which suggests uniqueness. I seem to remember that it was Douady who did this (he enjoyed playing with words); the date should be close to 1966, but I have not looked into his publications, and I cannot give you a precise reference.11 1 The earliest reference I have been able to find is [Dou60, p. 4]. Z.R.

That this idea applied to Galois cohomology was obvious from the beginning, both to people with a topologist background (such as Rost or myself), and to algebraists trying to parametrize equations (they rather used the word ‘‘generic’’, which I find a bit confusing. 22 2 See Remark 2.8. A.D. and Z.R.) But I don’t think(∗) the word ‘‘versal’’ got into print [in this context] before my UCLA lectures of 2001 (do you know an earlier reference?)33 3 The term versal is used in [BR97], Section 7. The versal polynomials defined there give rise to versal GG-torsors, in the sense of [Ser03, Section I.5], where GG is a finite group. Z.R., even though I had used it in some College lectures around 1990 (especially those on “negligible cohomology”, which were never written down).

Note that the definition in UCLA has a rather non standard restriction: it asks for a density property which may seem artificial (but it is essential in Duncan’s work!).

Best wishes,

J-P.Serre

(*) I have asked Google about “versal torsor”, but all the references there seem to be post 2001.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:
